content.statement: A test that saves a user to a real test database and reads it back is an integration test.

remember: As soon as a test runs your code together with a real database, network or file system, it is an integration test.

content.prompt: What does an integration test check that a unit test does not?

options.text: That one function returns the right value for a given input
That the screens look right in every supported browser
That your code works together with real dependencies, such as the database
That the code stays fast under heavy production load

remember: Unit tests check one piece in isolation; integration tests check that pieces and real dependencies work together.

content.prompt: Three of these are unit tests. Which one is an integration test?

items.text: slugify("Hello World") returns "hello-world"
UserRepository saves a user to a PostgreSQL test database and reads it back
The price calculator takes 10% off a 200 EUR order
validateEmail rejects "ana@"

remember: A test that needs a real database to run is an integration test; pure logic is checked with unit tests.

content.prompt: Match each bug with the cheapest kind of test that would catch it.

left.text: A migration renamed a column, but the repository's SQL still uses the old name
Checkout retries forever when the payment client throws
The reverse proxy strips the Authorization header before requests reach the API

right.text: An end-to-end test against the deployed app
A unit test of the function
An integration test against a real database
A unit test with a stubbed client that throws

remember: Pick the cheapest test that can see the bug: logic in unit tests, SQL in integration tests, wiring of the deployed parts end to end.

content.prompt: Your integration tests run the repositories against an in-memory SQLite database, while production runs PostgreSQL. What is the main risk?

options.text: In-memory SQLite is slower than PostgreSQL, so the suite drags
The tests stop being integration tests and become end-to-end tests
SQLite cannot run inside the same process as the tests
Tests can pass on SQL that PostgreSQL would reject or run differently

remember: Integration tests should use the same database engine as production; a stand-in hides dialect and constraint differences.

content.statement: In a healthy test pyramid, end-to-end tests are the most numerous kind of test.

remember: The pyramid has many unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests and only a few end-to-end tests at the top.

content.prompt: Why should unit tests make up the base of the test pyramid?

options.text: They catch every bug that end-to-end tests catch
They run in milliseconds and point straight at the broken code
They never need to change when the code changes
They exercise the real database and network

remember: Unit tests are cheap, fast and precise, so you can afford many of them; slower tests cover what units cannot see.

content.prompt: Order these tests of an online shop from the base of the test pyramid (most numerous, fastest) to the top.

steps.text: A browser signs in, fills the cart and pays
calculateTotal() returns the sum of the line prices
POST /api/orders on the running API returns 201 and stores the order
OrderRepository saves an order to a test database and reads it back

remember: The bigger the slice of the real system a test runs, the higher it sits in the pyramid and the fewer of them you write.

content.prompt: Three of these are signs of an upside-down test pyramid with too many end-to-end tests. Which one is not?

items.text: The full test suite takes 40 minutes to run
A red test rarely tells you which function broke
A unit test fails right after someone changes that function's logic
Tests often fail because a page loaded slowly

remember: Slow runs, vague failures and timing noise mean the suite leans on end-to-end tests; push those checks down to unit and integration tests.

content.prompt: For which service is it reasonable to write more integration tests than unit tests?

options.text: A thin CRUD API whose logic is mostly SQL queries and mapping rows to JSON
A tax engine that applies hundreds of rules in memory
A date parser that accepts many input formats
A pricing function that combines discounts and coupons

remember: The pyramid is a guide, not a law: when the behaviour lives in the database, integration tests give more confidence than unit tests with mocks.

content.statement: A test with no assertions is reported as passed as long as the code it calls does not throw.

remember: A test only fails when something throws or an assertion fails, so a test without assertions checks almost nothing.

content.prompt: getUser() returns a new object { id: 1, name: "Ana" }. Which assertion passes?

remember: toBe compares identity like ===, so two separate objects never match; use toEqual to compare their contents.

content.prompt: parse("") throws an Error with the message "empty input". Fill the blank so the test passes.

remember: toThrow needs a function it can call; passing parse("") runs it before expect, so the error escapes the assertion.

content.prompt: Someone deleted the amount check from withdraw, yet this test still passes. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Use toEqual instead of toBe to compare err.message
Replace the try/catch with expect(() => withdraw(account, -50)).toThrow("Amount must be positive")
Also assert expect(account.balance).toBe(100) inside the catch block

remember: An assertion inside catch only runs if something throws; assert the throw itself with expect(() => ...).toThrow().

content.prompt: Ignoring warnings, what happens when this script runs?

options.text: It raises AssertionError with no message
It raises TypeError, because assert cannot take a tuple

remember: assert (cond, "msg") asserts a non-empty tuple, which is always true; write assert cond, "msg" without parentheses.

content.statement: If a function works for a list of three items, also testing it with an empty list adds nothing.

remember: Empty input is one of the most common edge cases; test it on purpose, along with one item and the maximum.

content.prompt: A field accepts quantities from 1 to 99. Which set of test values best covers its boundaries?

remember: Test each limit and the value just outside it; off-by-one bugs live exactly there.

content.prompt: Every 10th item, such as the 10th, 20th and 30th, never shows up on any page. Find the bug.

remember: slice's end index is exclusive; test the first and last item of every page, where off-by-one bugs hide.

content.prompt: What does this print?
content.code:
def last_n(items, n):
    return items[-n:]


print(last_n([1, 2, 3], 2))
print(last_n([1, 2, 3], 0))

remember: -0 is just 0, so items[-0:] is the whole list; always test n = 0 for slicing helpers.

content.prompt: addMonth has an edge-case bug. Fill the blank with the input that exposes it by making this print a wrong date.

remember: Month ends are classic date edge cases: setMonth rolls 31 January over into March, so test the 31st and February.

content.statement: A unit test that replaces every collaborator with a mock also proves that the class works with the real collaborators.

remember: Mocks only behave the way you programmed them; integration tests are still needed to prove the real parts fit.

content.prompt: Which dependency is the best candidate to replace with a test double in a unit test?

options.text: A pure function that formats prices
An HTTP client that charges real credit cards

remember: Replace what is slow, external or has side effects, like payment or email APIs; keep fast, pure code real.

content.prompt: What does this print?
content.code:
from unittest.mock import Mock

rate = Mock(return_value=1.5)
print(rate("EUR"), rate("USD"), rate.call_count)

remember: A stubbed return value comes back for any arguments, and the mock counts every call so a test can check them.

content.prompt: Match each kind of test double with what it does.

right.text: Returns canned answers so the code under test can run
Checked afterwards for the calls the code was expected to make
A working but simplified implementation, such as an in-memory repository
Passed only to fill a parameter; never actually used

remember: Dummies fill parameters, stubs feed answers, mocks verify calls, and fakes are light working versions of the real thing.

content.prompt: The test still calls the real payment API, although charge is patched. Find the bug.

remember: Patch a name where it is looked up, not where it is defined: from x import f copies f into the importing module.

content.statement: Every test should pass when run on its own and in any order with the other tests.

remember: Tests that rely on each other's leftovers break when run alone, in parallel or in a different order.

content.prompt: Several tests need an empty shopping cart. Where should the cart be created?

options.text: In the first test; the later tests reuse it
In a beforeEach hook or fixture, so every test gets a new one
Once, in a global variable when the test file loads
In an afterAll hook at the end of the file

remember: Create fresh state for every test in beforeEach or a fixture; never let a test depend on what an earlier one left behind.

content.prompt: "a new cart is empty" fails when the whole file runs, but passes when it runs on its own. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Add afterAll(() => { cart = undefined; }) below it

remember: beforeAll shares one object across all tests; use beforeEach so each test starts from a clean state.

content.prompt: pytest runs both tests in file order. What does it report?

remember: A mutable default argument is shared between calls, so state leaks from one test into the next; default to None and build a new list.

content.prompt: A test file has a top-level beforeEach. Below it, a describe block holds a beforeAll, a beforeEach, an afterEach and then its first test. In what order do these run for that test?

steps.text: The describe block's beforeEach
The test itself
The top-level beforeEach
The describe block's afterEach
The describe block's beforeAll

remember: A block's beforeAll runs before any per-test hooks; then beforeEach hooks run outside-in and afterEach hooks inside-out.

content.statement: Rerunning a flaky test until it passes is a safe fix, because flakiness never points to a real bug.

remember: Flakiness can hide a real race condition or time bug; find the cause instead of retrying until green.

content.prompt: A test starts a background import, sleeps 200 ms, then checks that the rows exist. It fails now and then on busy CI machines. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Retry the test up to three times
Run this test first in the suite
Wait for the import to finish, or poll for the rows with a timeout

remember: A fixed sleep races against the machine's speed; wait for the actual condition instead.

content.prompt: What does this print?
content.code:
import random


def shuffled(items, seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    result = items[:]
    rng.shuffle(result)
    return result


a = shuffled([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], seed=42)
b = shuffled([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], seed=42)
print(a == b)

options.text: True on some runs and False on others

remember: A random generator with a fixed seed repeats the same sequence, so log the seed and reuse it to replay a failing random test.

content.prompt: On a laptop in Zagreb, this test fails when run shortly after midnight and passes the rest of the day. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Call date.today() before create_order and compare with that

remember: A UTC timestamp and the local date disagree for some hours of the day; compare in one time zone, or pass in a fixed clock.

content.prompt: Three of these tests are flaky. Which one is wrong but not flaky?

items.text: Asserts the order of strings read from a Python set
Asserts the row order of ORDER BY created_at when several rows share a timestamp
Two parallel workers start their test servers on the same fixed port
Expects 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 to be true

remember: A test that fails every time is just wrong; a flaky one depends on something that varies, such as hash order, ties in sorting or shared ports.

content.statement: In TDD, the code you write to make a test pass may be crude at first, because the refactor step cleans it up while the tests stay green.

remember: Green only has to pass the test; refactoring afterwards improves the design with the tests as a safety net.

content.prompt: What is the first step of each test-driven development cycle?

options.text: Write a small test that fails
Write the simplest code that could work

remember: Each TDD cycle starts red: a small test for the next behaviour, failing because the code does not exist yet.

content.prompt: In the red step this new test passed at once, although slugify did not handle spaces yet. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Call slugify only once and store the result

remember: Never compute the expected value with the code under test; write it out, and watch each new test fail first.

content.prompt: You test-drive total(cart), starting from the simplest case. In which order do you add these tests?

steps.text: A coupon bigger than the sum gives 0, not a negative total
A cart with one item totals that item's price
An empty cart totals 0
A 5 EUR coupon is taken off the sum of the items
A cart with several items totals the sum of their prices

remember: Grow the code in small steps: start with the simplest case, generalise one test at a time, then add the special rules.

content.prompt: Three of these are TDD habits. Which one goes against TDD?

items.text: Write the whole feature first, then add tests until coverage is high
Watch each new test fail before writing the code
Write only enough code to make the failing test pass
Refactor only while all tests are green

remember: In TDD the tests drive the code one small step at a time; tests written afterwards to raise coverage are not TDD.

content.statement: 100% line coverage means every behaviour of the code is checked by an assertion.

remember: Coverage only says which lines ran during the tests, not whether any assertion checked what they did.

content.prompt: The report shows 100% line coverage for finalPrice but only 50% branch coverage. What is missing?

options.text: An assertion on the returned price
A test where the price drops below zero
A test without a coupon, so the if condition is false
A second test with a different coupon amount

remember: Branch coverage needs every condition to go both ways; an if that is only ever true leaves half its branches untested.

content.prompt: Only this test runs. Which lines of shipping() does the coverage report mark as never executed?

remember: Missed lines in a coverage report show the paths no test took, here the foreign order and the small order.

content.prompt: Match each measure with what it counts.

right.text: Share of small deliberate code changes that made some test fail
Share of distinct routes through a function, combining all its decisions, that were run
Share of statements that ran at least once
Share of decision outcomes, such as both sides of each if, that were taken

remember: Statement and branch coverage count what ran, path coverage counts combinations of decisions, and a mutation score shows whether tests notice changed behaviour.

content.prompt: A mutation testing tool changed >= to > in isAdult, and the suite still passed. Fill the blank so the test passes on the real code but fails on the mutant.

remember: Full coverage can still miss a boundary; a surviving mutant points at the value, here exactly 18, that no test checks.

content.statement: End-to-end tests drive the application through its real interface, such as a browser, with the real backend behind it.

remember: End-to-end tests use the app the way a user does, so they catch wiring problems that isolated tests miss.

content.prompt: Which bug is an end-to-end test best placed to catch?

options.text: A helper that formats prices drops the cents
A sort function fails on an empty array
A regular expression accepts "ana@" as an email
The frontend calls /api/order while the API only serves /api/orders

remember: End-to-end tests are best at wiring bugs between parts; logic bugs inside one function are cheaper to catch with unit tests.

content.prompt: Order the stages of a CI pipeline so the fastest feedback comes first.

steps.text: Run integration tests against a database container
Run browser end-to-end tests against staging
Run the unit tests
Deploy the build to a staging environment

remember: Run cheap, fast tests first and the slow end-to-end tests last, once the build is deployed somewhere realistic.

content.prompt: Match each end-to-end test problem with its fix.

left.text: Breaks whenever designers rename CSS classes
Takes 40 minutes, so developers stop running it
A failure in CI cannot be understood from the log alone
Clicks Pay while the page is still loading and misses the button

right.text: Keep a few key journeys and move detailed rule checks to unit tests
Wait until the element is visible and enabled before acting
Find elements by role, label or a test id
Save a screenshot, video or trace when a test fails

remember: Keep end-to-end tests few and sturdy: user-facing selectors, waits for real conditions, and failure artifacts you can inspect.

content.prompt: This end-to-end test runs against a shared staging server many times a day, also in parallel CI jobs. Signup rejects an email that is already taken. Fill the blank so the test keeps passing.

remember: End-to-end tests share a real environment, so each run must create its own unique data instead of reusing fixed names.

content.statement: Changing several things at once is the fastest way to find out which change fixes a bug.

remember: Change one thing at a time; otherwise you cannot tell which change made the difference.

content.prompt: A bug appeared somewhere in the last 1,000 commits, and a test shows it. With git bisect, about how many commits do you need to test at most?

remember: Bisecting halves the search space at each step, so 1,000 commits need only about 10 tests.

content.prompt: Order these steps for fixing a bug that a user reported.

steps.text: Form a hypothesis about the cause
Fix it and add a regression test that failed before the fix
Reproduce the failure reliably
Run an experiment that could prove the hypothesis wrong
Shrink it to the smallest input that still fails

remember: Reproduce, shrink, form a hypothesis, test it, then fix with a regression test so the bug cannot quietly return.

content.prompt: One of 10,000 orders has a negative total and crashes process(). Fill the blank to pause in the debugger right before that order is processed.

remember: A conditional breakpoint stops only on the failing case, so you can inspect the state right before things go wrong.

content.prompt: Three of these narrow down where a bug is. Which one does not?

items.text: Bisecting the failing input file and retrying each half
Reverting only your local changes to see whether the bug remains
Upgrading every dependency at once and retrying
Logging the data halfway through the pipeline to see which half goes wrong

remember: Narrow a bug down by splitting the search space; changing many things at once only adds new suspects.

content.statement: In a Python traceback, the most recent call is printed last, just above the exception message.

remember: Python prints the oldest call first, so the frame that raised the error sits at the bottom, right above the message.

content.prompt: Signup crashes with this stack trace. Where should you start looking?
content.code:
TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'trim')
    at normalize (node_modules/mailkit/index.js:8:19)
    at createUser (src/users.js:41:17)
    at signup (src/routes.js:12:5)
    at Layer.handle (node_modules/express/lib/layer.js:95:5)

options.text: normalize in node_modules/mailkit, where the error was thrown
signup in src/routes.js, where the request came in
Layer.handle in express, at the bottom of the trace

remember: Start at the topmost frame from your own code: it usually passed the bad value into the library that threw.

content.prompt: The log shows only "charge failed for 42: timed out", with no stack trace, so nobody can tell which call timed out. Find the bug.

remember: Inside an except block, log.exception (or exc_info=True) records the full traceback; a plain message keeps only the text.

content.prompt: What does the traceback show when this runs?

options.text: Only the ValueError; the KeyError was caught, so it is gone
The KeyError, then "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:", then the ValueError
The KeyError, then "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:", then the ValueError

remember: Python keeps the exception you were handling and prints it first; use raise ... from err to mark it as the direct cause.

content.prompt: Match each log level with the kind of message it is for.

right.text: An operation failed, such as a payment that could not be charged
Something unexpected that the app recovered from, such as a retry
Detailed values for diagnosing a problem, usually off in production
A normal event worth recording, such as "order 42 created"

remember: DEBUG is for diagnostic detail, INFO for normal events, WARNING for recovered surprises and ERROR for failed operations.
